hook.support: Road safety ads used to show crashes and crying families. In 2016, the TAC made a strange sculpture called Graham. He was built to survive a crash. Did he work on your head, or your heart?
hook.core: For years, road safety ads showed crashes, crying families and funerals. Then in 2016, Victoria's TAC tried something different: a strange, life-size human sculpture called Graham, built to survive a car crash. It used science to make a point, and it was hard to forget. Was it working on your head, or your heart?

why.support: Ads and speeches try to change your mind. Some use facts. Some use feelings. The best use both. Learn to spot them, and use them yourself.
why.core: Every ad, speech and campaign is trying to change your mind. Some use **logic**: facts and reasons. Some use **emotion**: stories, pictures and feelings. The best use both. When you can see how they're working on you, you can decide for yourself. And you can use the same tools when it's your turn to persuade.
why.extend: Persuasive texts work on audiences through logic, reasoning and emotion, delivered through structures that suit their form: written, spoken or multimedia. Recognising how these appeals work, and where reasoning breaks down, lets you evaluate arguments and build stronger ones.

articles.title: Head or heart?

body.support:
Ads and speeches want you to think or do something. They work on your **head**, your **heart**, or both.

**Logic: the head.** Logic uses facts and numbers. *“Seatbelts save lives.”*

**Reasons.** Good reasons link ideas with *because* and *so*. *“Alcohol slows you down, **so** it takes longer to stop.”*

**Emotion: the heart.** Emotion uses stories, faces and music. It makes you feel sad, scared or proud. A photo of an empty chair at dinner can hit hard.

**Bad reasons.** Some reasons sound right but aren't:

- **“Everyone's doing it.”** That doesn't make it right.
- **“Don't listen to her, she's only 16.”** That's about her, not her idea.
- **“If we let this happen, everything will fall apart.”** That's a big jump.

**How ads are set out.** Many video ads go: a hook, a problem, some reasons, then a **call to action**: what to do.

The best ads use head and heart. Feelings grab you. Facts give you a reason.
body.core:
Every ad, speech and campaign wants you to think or do something. To get there, it works on your **head**, your **heart**, or both.

**Logic: the head.** Logic uses facts, numbers and evidence. *“Seatbelts reduce the risk of dying in a crash.”* It asks you to think it through.

**Reasoning: the links.** Reasoning joins ideas together with words like *because*, *so* and *therefore*. *“Alcohol slows your reactions, **so** it takes longer to stop, **so** you're more likely to crash.”* Good reasoning is easy to follow, one step at a time.

**Emotion: the heart.** Emotion uses stories, faces, music and strong words to make you *feel*: fear, sadness, pride, anger, hope. A photo of an empty chair at a family dinner can hit harder than any number.

**Faulty reasoning.** Some arguments sound right but don't add up. Watch out for:

- **“Everyone's doing it.”** Lots of people doing something doesn't make it right.
- **Slippery slope.** *“If we allow this, soon everything will fall apart.”*
- **Attacking the person.** *“Don't listen to her, she's only 16.”* That says nothing about her idea.
- **False choice.** *“You're either with us or against us.”* There are usually more options.

**Structure.** Persuasive texts are built in a pattern. A **written** opinion piece has a contention, arguments and a conclusion. A **speech** has an opening that grabs, a few clear points, and a strong finish. A **video ad** often goes: hook, problem, reasons, then a **call to action**. Music, images and text on screen do a lot of the work.

The strongest arguments use both head and heart. Emotion grabs your attention. Logic gives you a reason to act.
body.extend:
Every persuasive text aims to change what its audience thinks or does. It does this by appealing to the **head**, the **heart**, or both.

**Logic.** Logical appeals rely on facts, statistics and evidence. *“Seatbelts reduce the risk of dying in a crash.”* They invite the audience to think it through.

**Reasoning.** Reasoning connects claims in a chain, signalled by *because*, *so* and *therefore*. *“Alcohol slows reaction time, **so** stopping distance increases, **so** the risk of a crash rises.”* Strong reasoning is explicit and easy to follow.

**Emotion.** Emotional appeals use stories, faces, music, images and emotive language to provoke fear, grief, pride, anger or hope. A single image, such as an empty chair at a family dinner, can carry more force than a statistic.

**Faulty reasoning.** Some arguments are persuasive but flawed:

- **Bandwagon:** popularity doesn't prove something is right.
- **Slippery slope:** a small step is claimed to lead, without evidence, to disaster.
- **Attacking the person:** criticising the speaker instead of the argument.
- **False choice:** presenting two options when others exist.

**Structure and form.** Persuasive content takes different shapes. A **written** opinion piece moves from contention to arguments to conclusion. A **spoken** speech opens strongly, develops a few clear points, and closes memorably. A **multimedia** ad often follows hook, problem, reasons and **call to action**, with images, sound and on-screen text carrying much of the meaning.

The most effective arguments combine appeals. Emotion captures attention. Logic and reasoning give the audience a reason to act.

caseStudies.title: Meet Graham

body.support:
The **TAC** makes road safety ads in Victoria. For years, its ads showed crashes and sad families.

In **2016**, it tried something new. It made **Graham**. Graham is a life-size sculpture of a body that could survive a car crash.

An artist made him. She worked with a surgeon and a crash expert. They worked out what a body would need to survive.

Graham looks very strange. He has a huge, thick skull. He has airbags between his ribs.

The TAC said Graham shows how easily our real bodies get hurt on the road.

Graham used **facts**: real science about crashes. He used **feelings**: he's strange and hard to forget. Head and heart.
body.core:
For years, Victoria's **Transport Accident Commission (TAC)** was known for road safety ads. Many showed the shock of a crash, and what came after.

In **July 2016**, it tried something new. It unveiled **Graham**: a life-size sculpture of a human body built to survive a car crash.

Melbourne artist **Patricia Piccinini** made Graham. She worked with **Christian Kenfield**, a surgeon at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. She also worked with **David Logan**, a crash expert from Monash University. Together they worked out how a body would need to change to survive a crash.

The result looks strange, even disturbing. Graham has a huge, thick skull that folds over the front of his face. He has airbag-like sacs between his ribs to protect his organs.

The TAC said the point was to show how easily our real bodies get hurt on the road. It also said safer cars and roads make crashes less violent, so more people survive.

Graham was first shown at the **State Library of Victoria**, then toured the state.

The campaign used **logic**: real science about crash forces. It used **emotion**: a body so odd that it's hard to look at, and hard to forget. Head and heart, together.
body.extend:
Victoria's **Transport Accident Commission (TAC)** had long been known for road safety advertising built on the shock of crashes and their aftermath.

In **July 2016**, it took a different approach. It unveiled **Graham**, a life-size sculpture of a human body designed to survive a car crash.

Melbourne artist **Patricia Piccinini** created Graham. She worked with trauma surgeon **Christian Kenfield** and crash investigator **David Logan**. Together they worked out how a body would need to change to survive a crash.

The result is unsettling. Graham has a huge, thick skull that folds over his face. He has airbag-like sacs between his ribs.

The TAC said the aim was to remind people how **vulnerable** they are on the road. It also made a logical case. Safer cars and better road design can reduce crash forces, so more crashes are survivable.

Graham was first displayed at the **State Library of Victoria**, then toured the state.

The campaign combined appeals. Its **logic** rested on medical and engineering evidence. Its **emotional** force came from an image so strange that audiences found it hard to forget.

teacher.overview: Students learn how authors and speakers use logic, reasoning and emotion to influence an audience; how to spot faulty reasoning (bandwagon, slippery slope, attacking the person, false choice); how language, images and sound contribute to an argument; and how written, spoken and multimedia persuasive texts are structured. They annotate a made-up video ad script, sort strong from faulty reasoning, write head and heart lines, and pull apart a real ad. The case study is the TAC's 2016 Graham campaign: a sculpture of a body built to survive a crash, created by artist Patricia Piccinini with a trauma surgeon and a crash investigator.
prep: Pick two or three real ads to model (TAC campaigns are on YouTube; also try a charity or health campaign).
Optional: show images of Graham from the TAC website.
Check sound works on student devices for the Do it.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** logic uses facts and evidence (head); emotion uses stories, images and music to make you feel (heart). E.g. bandwagon, slippery slope, attacking the person, false choice. Hook, problem, reasons, call to action.

**Ad script:** 1 hook (heart); 2 speaks to the audience (heart); 3 logic (head); 4 reasoning chain (head); 5 emotion (heart, silence adds weight); 6 call to action (both).

**Sort:** phone — faulty (bandwagon); seatbelts — strong; phones at lunch — faulty (slippery slope); pool survey — strong; Jay — faulty (attacks the person); highway — faulty (false choice).

**Case study:** logic: science of crash forces, designed with a surgeon and crash investigator; emotion: a disturbing, unforgettable body. Audiences may have become used to crash ads. Answers will vary.

resources.label: Smithsonian Magazine — sculpture of a human evolved to survive a car crash

realityCheck: **Road trauma may be personal.** Some students may have lost someone; the Graham case is less graphic than crash ads, but check in.
**Students know ads.** Let them bring their own; they'll be sharper critics than you expect.
**Faulty reasoning is everywhere.** Challenge students to catch one in class discussion (kindly).
**Don't over-praise logic.** Emotion isn't bad; the question is whether it's backed up.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It builds on Back It Up and leads into Say It Like You Mean It.
